    Cache¶

    How .ligase/ is laid out, how a key is composed, and what each choice costs. The user-facing account is Running, and not running.

    Everything here lives in crates/ligase-core/src/: hash.rs, key.rs and cache.rs. None of it knows about Python.

    The directory¶

    .ligase/
├── cache.sqlite          metadata: keys, outputs, file hashes
├── store/                content-addressed objects
│   └── 3c/73431de6...eeaa85.tsv
└── tmp/                  staging, for steps that are still running

    Three properties are deliberate.

    The store is fanned out over the first byte of the hash. A cohort of four hundred samples through five steps is two thousand objects; a flat directory of those is a directory no filesystem enjoys. One level of 256 buckets is enough for the sizes this tool is for.

    An object keeps its suffix. samtools sort -o x.bam writes BAM and x.sam writes SAM: tools read the format off the name, so an object called 3c73… with no extension is an object no tool will read correctly. Everything after the first dot survives, which is what keeps .vcf.gz intact.

    Staging is inside the cache directory. Moving a finished output into the store is then a rename rather than a copy — a 24 GB BAM copied once more per run would be a real cost — and a crashed run leaves its debris somewhere a user can delete wholesale.

    Stored objects are made read-only. The store is the cache's evidence: a step that wrote back through one of its inputs would invalidate every key derived from it without anything noticing.

    The schema¶

    CREATE TABLE meta  (name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value TEXT NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE files (path TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                    size INTEGER NOT NULL,
                    mtime_ns INTEGER NOT NULL,
                    hash TEXT NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE steps (key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                    step TEXT NOT NULL,
                    output_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
                    suffix TEXT NOT NULL,
                    tools TEXT NOT NULL,
                    duration_ms INTEGER NOT NULL,
                    created_at TEXT NOT NULL);

    SQLite because D6 says so: zero-config, embedded, portable, and — the part that matters for a reproducibility tool — openable with sqlite3 when a result needs explaining. A faster key-value store that can only be read by the program that wrote it would be a worse trade here.

    rusqlite is used with the bundled feature, which compiles SQLite from source. That costs a C compiler at build time, which is a real concession given that D11 chose pure-Rust format parsing precisely to avoid one. It buys one identical SQLite everywhere, which an on-disk format that outlives a single run needs more than it needs a shorter build.

    duration_ms and tools are not used for cache decisions. They are there because the next question after "was this cached?" is "how long did it take when it did run, and with what?" — and because M5 will want them.

    Versioning, and why nothing is migrated¶

    Two version numbers sit in meta.

    schema_version describes the directory layout. A directory written by another version has its tables dropped.

    key_version describes how keys are composed (key::KEY_VERSION). A mismatch deletes every row of steps, and keeps files.

    That asymmetry is the whole point. A file's hash is a fact about the file, true regardless of how keys are made. A step's entry is a claim that these ingredients, combined this way produced that output — so a key from another format is not stale data to be migrated, it is a claim about something else. Reading it would be the one failure mode a cache must never have.

    Nothing is migrated because nothing needs to be: every byte in here is derived, and the cost of being wrong is enormously higher than the cost of recomputing.

    The prefilter¶

    Cache::content_hash consults files by (path, size, mtime_ns). A hit returns the stored hash without opening the file; a miss hashes it and records the result.

    Three details keep this honest.

    A timestamp can only ever save work. It never contributes to a hash and never to a key. The direction of the bet matters: a stale timestamp causes a rehash (a cost), never a wrong answer — except in the one case below.

    The file is re-stat'd after hashing. A file written while we were hashing it would otherwise be remembered under the size and mtime it had before, and every later run would trust that hash. If the stat moved, the hash is used for this run and not recorded.

    The miss case is a file edited in place, keeping its exact length, within one timestamp granularity. This is the residual risk of D3, it is documented rather than hidden, and --force is the answer. The alternative — hashing every input on every run — makes looking at a 40 GB BAM cost minutes, which turns content addressing from a feature into something users route around.

    Cache::stats() counts hits and misses, which is where report.hashed and report.prefiltered come from. It exists so the prefilter is testable: asserting that a second run read nothing is how you find out it is working, and no amount of staring at output tells you that.

    The key¶

    pub struct Ingredients {
    pub step: String,                      // the step's name
    pub code: String,                      // its source, as written
    pub recipe: String,                    // the command, or "callback"
    pub output: DataKind,                  // what it declares it produces
    pub parameters: Vec<(String, String)>, // (name, value)
    pub inputs: Vec<(String, ContentHash)>,// (parameter, content hash)
    pub tools: Vec<(String, String)>,      // (name, version)
}

    Hashed with BLAKE3, every field length-prefixed. The length prefixes are not decoration: concatenating would make a parameter x with value yz indistinguishable from a parameter xy with value z, and a cache key that can confuse two different inputs is a wrong answer waiting for the right coincidence. There is a test for exactly that pair.

    Names bind, order does not. Inputs, parameters and tools are sorted by name before hashing, so the order they were collected in cannot change a key — but which name a value is bound to very much does, because the same two files swapped between aln and ref is a different command.

    The composition is pinned by a test that asserts a literal key for a fixed set of ingredients. That makes an accidental change to the layout a failing test rather than a silently cold cache for every user of the release; it is meant to be updated deliberately, together with KEY_VERSION.

    code is the function's source as written, read with inspect.getsource. The consequence is worth stating plainly: a comment-only edit reruns the step. That is the safe direction — too cold costs time, too warm produces a wrong answer — and early cutoff stops the rerun going any further. For a function with no source to read (a REPL, an exec), the compiled code object stands in.

    What an input's hash is a hash of¶

    Inputs enter as content hashes tagged with the policy that produced them. Since M4 that is INPUT_POLICY = "canonical": the hash of what a file means rather than of its bytes (D4) — sorted records, volatile headers such as @PG lines and timestamps stripped, as canonicalisation defines per type.

    It arrived exactly as this page said it would, which is worth recording because it was the point of putting the tag in before needing it: the policy name changed, KEY_VERSION went to 2, the old entries retired themselves, and nothing in the shape of Ingredients moved. Runner::key asks Cache::semantic_hash(kind, path) where it asked Cache::content_hash.

    Three things sit in meta now rather than two, and they are cleared differently. A layout change drops the tables; a key-format change deletes the step entries; a change to the canonicalisation rules (CANON_VERSION) deletes the canonical hashes and the step entries built from them. The files table survives all three, because a file's byte hash is a fact about the file however keys are made.

    The store still names objects after their bytes, deliberately: an object's name is a claim about its contents that anyone can check with b3sum. The canonical hash is a derived fact held beside it, in the canonical table, keyed on the byte hash rather than on a path — so a file moved, copied, or produced identically by another step is parsed once in its life.

    What is not here¶

    Provenance. This layer records that a key produced an output, with the tool versions and the duration, because it had them. It does not record why a result is what it is — the command, the references, the citations, the methods paragraph. That lives in provenance.sqlite, beside this database and deliberately not in it: "has this been computed?" and "what would I write in a paper?" want different lifetimes, and this one's tables are dropped whenever a key format moves (D23). See provenance.
